{{Short description|Graph which can be made planar by removing a single node}}
[[File:Apex graph.svg|thumb|An apex graph. The [[Glossary of graph theory#Subgraphs|subgraph]] formed by removing the red vertex is [[planar graph|planar]].]]

In [[graph theory]], a branch of mathematics, an '''apex graph''' is a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] that can be made [[planar graph|planar]] by the removal of a single [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertex]]. The deleted vertex is called an apex of the graph. It is ''an'' apex, not ''the'' apex because an apex graph may have more than one apex; for example, in the minimal nonplanar graphs {{math|''K''{{sub|5}}}} or {{math|''K''{{sub|3,3}}}}, every vertex is an apex. The apex graphs include graphs that are themselves planar, in which case again every vertex is an apex. The [[null graph]] is also counted as an apex graph even though it has no vertex to remove.

Apex graphs are [[closure (mathematics)|closed]] under the operation of taking [[graph minor|minors]] and play a role in several other aspects of graph minor theory: [[linkless embedding]],<ref name="linkless"/> [[Hadwiger conjecture (graph theory)|Hadwiger's conjecture]],<ref name="rst93">{{harvtxt|Robertson|Seymour|Thomas|1993a}}.</ref> YΔY-reducible graphs,<ref name="t92"/> and relations between [[treewidth]] and [[Diameter (graph theory)|graph diameter]].<ref name="local"/>

==Characterization and recognition==
Apex graphs are [[closure (mathematics)|closed]] under the operation of taking [[graph minor|minors]]: contracting any edge, or removing any edge or vertex, leads to another apex graph. For, if {{mvar|G}} is an apex graph with apex {{mvar|v}}, then any contraction or removal that does not involve {{mvar|v}} preserves the planarity of the remaining graph, as does any edge removal of an edge incident to {{mvar|v}}. If an edge incident to {{mvar|v}} is contracted, the effect on the remaining graph is equivalent to the removal of the other endpoint of the edge. And if {{mvar|v}} itself is removed, any other vertex may be chosen as the apex.<ref name="gi91"/>

By the [[Robertson–Seymour theorem]], because they form a minor-closed family of graphs, the apex graphs have a [[forbidden graph characterization]].
There are only finitely many graphs that are neither apex graphs nor have another non-apex graph as a minor.
These graphs are ''forbidden minors'' for the property of being an apex graph.
Any other graph {{mvar|G}} is an apex graph [[if and only if]] none of the forbidden minors is a minor of {{mvar|G}}.
These forbidden minors include the seven graphs of the [[Petersen family]], three disconnected graphs formed from the disjoint unions of two of {{math|''K''{{sub|5}}}} and {{math|''K''{{sub|3,3}}}}, and many other graphs. However, a complete description of them remains unknown.<ref name="gi91">{{harvtxt|Gupta|Impagliazzo|1991}}.</ref>{{sfnp|Pierce|2014}}

Despite the complete set of forbidden minors remaining unknown, it is possible to test whether a given graph is an apex graph, and if so, to find an apex for the graph, in [[linear time]]. More generally, for any fixed constant {{mvar|k}}, it is possible to recognize in linear time the '''{{mvar|k}}-apex graphs''', the graphs in which the removal of some carefully chosen set of at most {{mvar|k}} vertices leads to a planar graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Kawarabayashi|2009}}.</ref> If {{mvar|k}} is variable, however, the problem is [[NP-complete]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Lewis|Yannakakis|1980}}.</ref>

==Chromatic number==
Every apex graph has [[graph coloring|chromatic number]] at most five: the underlying planar graph requires at most four colors by the [[four color theorem]], and the remaining vertex needs at most one additional color. {{harvtxt|Robertson|Seymour|Thomas|1993a}} used this fact in their proof of the case {{math|1=''k'' = 6}} of the [[Hadwiger conjecture (graph theory)|Hadwiger conjecture]], the statement that every 6-chromatic graph has the [[complete graph]] {{math|''K''{{sub|6}}}} as a minor: they showed that any minimal [[counterexample]] to the conjecture would have to be an apex graph, but since there are no 6-chromatic apex graphs such a counterexample cannot exist.

{{unsolved|mathematics|Is every 6-vertex-connected {{math|''K''{{sub|6}}}}-minor-free graph an apex graph?}}
{{harvtxt|Jørgensen|1994}} conjectured that every [[K-vertex-connected graph|6-vertex-connected]] graph that does not have {{math|''K''{{sub|6}}}} as a minor must be an apex graph. If this were proved, the Robertson–Seymour–Thomas result on the Hadwiger conjecture would be an immediate consequence.<ref name="rst93"/> Jørgensen's conjecture remains unproven.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/jorgensens_conjecture|title=Jorgensen's Conjecture|work=Open Problem Garden|accessdate=2016-11-13}}.</ref> However, if false, it has only finitely many counterexamples.{{sfnp|Kawarabayashi|Norine|Thomas|Wollan|2012}}

==Local treewidth==
A graph family {{mvar|F}} has ''bounded local treewidth'' if the graphs in {{mvar|F}} obey a functional relationship between [[distance (graph theory)|diameter]] and [[treewidth]]: there exists a function {{mvar|f}} such that the treewidth of a diameter-{{mvar|d}} graph in {{mvar|F}} is at most {{math|''f'' (''d'')}}. The apex graphs do not have bounded local treewidth: the apex graphs formed by connecting an apex vertex to every vertex of an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} [[grid graph]] have treewidth {{mvar|n}} and diameter 2, so the treewidth is not bounded by a function of diameter for these graphs. However, apex graphs are intimately connected to bounded local treewidth: the minor-closed graph families {{mvar|F}} that have bounded local treewidth are exactly the families that have an apex graph as one of their forbidden minors.<ref name="local">{{harvtxt|Eppstein|2000}}; {{harvtxt|Demaine|Hajiaghayi|2004}}.</ref> A minor-closed family of graphs that has an apex graph as one of its forbidden minors is known as ''apex-minor-free''. With this terminology, the connection between apex graphs and local treewidth can be restated as the fact that apex-minor-free graph families are the same as minor-closed graph families with bounded local treewidth.

The concept of bounded local treewidth forms the basis of the theory of [[bidimensionality]], and allows for many algorithmic problems on apex-minor-free graphs to be solved exactly by a polynomial-time algorithm or a [[fixed-parameter tractability|fixed-parameter tractable]] algorithm, or approximated using a [[polynomial-time approximation scheme]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Eppstein|2000}}; {{harvtxt|Frick|Grohe|2001}}; {{harvtxt|Demaine|Hajiaghayi|2005}}.</ref> Apex-minor-free graph families obey a strengthened version of the [[graph structure theorem]], leading to additional approximation algorithms for [[graph coloring]] and the [[travelling salesman problem]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Demaine|Hajiaghayi|Kawarabayashi|2009}}.</ref> However, some of these results can also be extended to arbitrary minor-closed graph families via structure theorems relating them to apex-minor-free graphs.<ref>{{harvtxt|Grohe|2003}}.</ref>

==Embeddings==
If {{mvar|G}} is an apex graph with apex {{mvar|v}}, and {{math|τ}} is the minimum number of faces needed to cover all the neighbors of {{mvar|v}} in a planar embedding of {{math|''G'' \ {''v''},}} then {{mvar|G}} may be embedded onto a two-dimensional surface of [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] {{math|τ – 1}}: simply add that number of bridges to the planar embedding, connecting together all the faces into which {{mvar|v}} must be connected. For instance, adding a single vertex to an [[outerplanar graph]] (a graph with {{math|1=τ = 1}}) produces a planar graph. When {{math|''G'' \ {''v''} }} is 3-connected, this bound is within a constant factor of optimal: every surface embedding of {{mvar|G}} requires genus at least {{math|{{sfrac|τ|160}}}}. However, it is [[NP-hard]] to determine the optimal genus of a surface embedding of an apex graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Mohar|2001}}.</ref>

By using [[SPQR tree]]s to encode the possible embeddings of the planar part of an apex graph, it is possible to compute a [[graph drawing|drawing]] of the graph in the plane in which the only crossings involve the apex vertex, minimizing the total number of crossings, in polynomial time.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chimani|Gutwenger|Mutzel|Wolf|2009}}.</ref> However, if arbitrary crossings are allowed, it becomes NP-hard to minimize the number of crossings, even in the special case of apex graphs formed by adding a single edge to a planar graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Cabello|Mohar|2010}}.</ref>

Apex graphs are also [[linkless embedding|linklessly embeddable]] in [[three-dimensional space]]: they can be embedded in such a way that each cycle in the graph is the boundary of a disk that is not crossed by any other feature of the graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Robertson|Seymour|Thomas|1993c}}.</ref> A drawing of this type may be obtained by drawing the planar part of the graph in a plane, placing the apex above the plane, and connecting the apex by straight-line edges to each of its neighbors. Linklessly embeddable graphs form a minor-closed family with the seven graphs in the [[Petersen family]] as their minimal forbidden minors;<ref name="linkless">{{harvtxt|Robertson|Seymour|Thomas|1993b}}.</ref> therefore, these graphs are also forbidden as minors for the apex graphs. However, there exist linklessly embeddable graphs that are not apex graphs.

==YΔY-reducibility==
[[File:Apex rhombic dodecahedron.svg|thumb|Robertson's example of a non-YΔY-reducible apex graph.]]
A connected graph is YΔY-reducible if it can be reduced to a single vertex by a sequence of steps, each of which is a [[Y-Δ transform|Δ-Y or Y-Δ transform]], the removal of a self-loop or multiple adjacency, the removal of a vertex with one neighbor, and the replacement of a vertex of degree two and its two neighboring edges by a single edge.<ref name="t92">{{harvtxt|Truemper|1992}}.</ref>

Like the apex graphs and the linkless embeddable graphs, the YΔY-reducible graphs are closed under graph minors. And, like the linkless embeddable graphs, the YΔY-reducible graphs have the seven graphs in the [[Petersen family]] as forbidden minors, prompting the question of whether these are the only forbidden minors and whether the YΔY-reducible graphs are the same as the linkless embeddable graphs. However, Neil Robertson provided an example of an apex graph that is not YΔY-reducible. Since every apex graph is linkless embeddable, this shows that there are graphs that are linkless embeddable but not YΔY-reducible and therefore that there are additional forbidden minors for the YΔY-reducible graphs.<ref name="t92"/>

Robertson's apex graph is shown in the figure. It can be obtained by connecting an apex vertex to each of the degree-three vertices of a [[rhombic dodecahedron]], or by merging two diametrally opposed vertices of a four-dimensional [[hypercube graph]]. Because the rhombic dodecahedron's graph is planar, Robertson's graph is an apex graph. It is a [[triangle-free graph]] with minimum [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] four, so it cannot be changed by any YΔY-reduction.<ref name="t92"/>

==Nearly planar graphs==
[[File:Moebius-ladder-16.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|The 16-vertex [[Möbius ladder]], an example of a nearly planar graph.]]
If a graph is an apex graph, it is not necessarily the case that it has a unique apex. For instance, in the minor-minimal nonplanar graphs ''K''<sub>5</sub> and ''K''<sub>3,3</sub>, any of the vertices can be chosen as the apex. {{harvs|last=Wagner|year=1967|year2=1970|txt}} defined a '''nearly planar graph''' to be a nonplanar apex graph with the property that all vertices can be the apex of the graph; thus, ''K''<sub>5</sub> and ''K''<sub>3,3</sub> are nearly planar. He provided a classification of these graphs into four subsets, one of which consists of the graphs that (like the [[Möbius ladder]]s) can be embedded onto the [[Möbius strip]] in such a way that the single edge of the strip coincides with a [[Hamiltonian cycle]] of the graph. Prior to the proof of the [[four color theorem]], he proved that every nearly planar graph can be colored with at most four colors, except for the graphs formed from a [[wheel graph]] with an odd outer cycle by replacing the hub vertex with two adjacent vertices, which require five colors. Additionally, he proved that, with a single exception (the eight-vertex [[complement graph]] of the [[cube]]) every nearly planar graph has an embedding onto the [[projective plane]].

However, the phrase "nearly planar graph" is highly ambiguous: it has also been used to refer to apex graphs,<ref>{{harvtxt|Robertson|Seymour|Thomas|1993c}}; {{harvtxt|Eppstein|2000}}.</ref> graphs formed by adding one edge to a planar graph,<ref>{{harvtxt|Archdeacon|Bonnington|2004}}.</ref> and graphs formed from a planar embedded graph by replacing a bounded number of faces by "vortexes" of bounded [[pathwidth]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Abraham|Gavoille|2006}}.</ref> as well as for other less precisely defined sets of graphs.

==Related graph classes==
An abstract graph is said to be ''n''-apex if it can be made planar by deleting ''n'' or fewer vertices. A 1-apex graph is also said to be apex.

According to {{harvtxt|Lipton|Mackall|Mattman|Pierce|2018}}, a graph is '''edge-apex''' if there is some edge in the graph that can be deleted to make the graph planar. A graph is '''contraction-apex''' if there is some edge in the graph that can be contracted to make the graph planar.

In general, if '''X''' is a class of graphs, an "apex-'''X'''" graph is a graph that can be brought into the class '''X''' by deleting some one vertex.  For example, an apex-[[cograph]] is a graph ''G'' that has a vertex ''v'' such that ''G―v'' is a cograph.

==See also==
*[[Polyhedral pyramid]], a 4-dimensional polytope whose vertices and edges form an apex graph, with the apex adjacent to every vertex of a [[polyhedral graph]]
